title: Breakfast rolls at a bakery in Berlin
setting: It's Sunday morning in Prenzlauer Berg, Berlin. Most shops are closed, but the neighbourhood Bäckerei is open and busy. Behind the glass counter: rows of bread rolls, pretzels and cakes.
objectives: Learn what Berliners call a bread roll — and why it changes by region
Understand "Sonst noch etwas?" and finish your order
Know what to expect when paying
varietyNote: This is standard German as heard in Berlin, with one local favourite: "Schrippe" for a bread roll. German varies a lot by region — the same roll is a "Brötchen" in much of Germany, a "Semmel" in Bavaria and Austria, and a "Weckle" in Swabia. Standard German is understood everywhere.

phrases.text: Ich hätte gern zwei Schrippen, bitte.
phrases.translation: I'd like two bread rolls, please.
phrases.example: Ich hätte gern ein Croissant und eine Brezel, bitte.
phrases.exampleTranslation: I'd like a croissant and a pretzel, please.
phrases.note: "Ich hätte gern…" (I would like…) is the standard polite way to order.

phrases.example: —Zum Mitnehmen oder zum hier Essen? —Zum Mitnehmen.
phrases.exampleTranslation: "To take away or to eat here?" "To take away."

phrases.example: Entschuldigung, kann ich mit Karte zahlen?
phrases.exampleTranslation: Excuse me, can I pay by card?

cultureNotes: Cash is still more common in Germany than in many countries. Small bakeries increasingly take cards, but it's wise to carry some cash — and to ask first.
Most shops are closed on Sundays, but many bakeries open on Sunday mornings for fresh rolls.
Service can feel brisk and direct. That's efficiency, not rudeness.
The word for a bread roll is a famous regional marker — Germans will happily debate whether it's a Schrippe, Brötchen, Semmel or Weckle.

steps.text: You reach the counter. The baker wipes her hands on her apron.

steps.speaker: Baker
steps.translation: Good morning! What would you like?

steps.prompt: You'd like two bread rolls. How do you order, Berlin-style?

options.text: Ich hätte gern zwei Schrippen, bitte.
options.why: Polite, natural — and "Schrippen" is the local Berlin word. "Zwei Brötchen" works too.
"Ich will" (I want) sounds pushy in a shop. Use "Ich hätte gern…" or "Ich möchte…".
"Brot" is a whole loaf of bread. For rolls, ask for Schrippen or Brötchen.
The standard question at the end of an order.
"Süß" means sweet — this is a general "anything else?".

options.text: Is that all the money you have?
options.why: Nothing to do with money — she's asking if you'd like anything else.

steps.prompt: That's all you need. What do you say?

options.why: Friendly and natural: "No thanks, that's all."
"Done!" sounds abrupt, like announcing you've finished a task.
"Nothing more, forever" — dramatic! A simple "Das wär's" is what you need.

steps.prompt: You're taking them home. How do you answer?

options.why: "Wegnehmen" means "to take something away from someone" — not what you mean.
You might be understood in Berlin, but in German it's "zum Mitnehmen".

steps.prompt: You only have a card on you. What's the best thing to do?

options.text: Ask "Kann ich mit Karte zahlen?" — many small bakeries take cards now, but not all.
options.why: Right. Asking first avoids an awkward moment, and carrying a little cash in Germany is still a good idea.

options.text: Just tap your card — Germany is completely cashless.
options.why: Germany still uses a lot of cash, especially in small shops. Ask first.

options.text: Leave without paying and come back later.
options.why: Never needed — just ask about card payment, or find a cash machine and come back.

steps.speaker: Baker
steps.translation: Yes, of course. Have a nice rest of your Sunday!
